## **Barrios Visibles, Part III: Yes, Three Million Missing is Plausible**

In my working paper and a subsequent blog post, I argued that open building footprints data suggest that something like 3 million people living in informal settlements are unaccounted for in Argentina’s RENABAP and INDEC censuses. In this post, I explore that claim in depth and discuss:

1. How we know that millions of people don’t show up in the 2022 INDEC Census.  
2. Why building footprints are a reliable proxy for households in informal settlements.  
3. Why a gap of this size is actually way more believable than it sounds.  
4. Why other explanations fail to account for such a large discrepancy.  
5. Why historical evidence and limitations on INDEC’s part make an undercount of this magnitude plausible.

TL;DR, the numbers are credible, nothing else I’ve found explains such a large gap, and there is a lot of precedent that suggests that the 2022 INDEC Census genuinely could be off by several million people.

**Millions of people are not where they should be**

First, a quick recap for those who didn’t read the working paper: Argentina’s Registro Nacional de Barrios Populares (or, [RENABAP](https://www.argentina.gob.ar/obras-publicas/sisu/renabap)) appears to be underestimating the population of informal settlements by about three million people. RENABAP’s data are distinct from INDEC’s 

This is distinct from Argentina’s national census, which is published roughly every ten years by INDEC (the Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos), although they do rely on a similar network of enumerators and community experts to do their counting in informal settlements.

Let’s start with a simple observation: there are way more building footprints in Argentina’s informal settlements than INDEC’s 2022 Census reports households. (INDEC, for those who haven’t read my working paper, is Argentina’s [National Institute of Statistics and Censuses](https://www.indec.gob.ar/).) This is abundantly clear in images of Census tracts that fall within informal settlements, e.g.,

![][image1]

We can actually calculate this difference. While INDEC’s Census tracts don’t usually correspond cleanly to informal settlement boundaries, there are a couple of ways around this.

The simplest option is to look at Census tracts that fall completely (or almost completely) inside informal settlements, which gives us a clear indication of how many households the Census reports relative to the number of footprints. I looked at 738 Census tracts that are at least 95% covered by RENABAP boundaries, across 515 informal settlements. In these tracts, there are 346,621 building footprints, compared to 224,278 households reported by the Census, or about 0.65 Census-reported households for every visible building footprint. Because we know that there are 1.97 million building footprints contained in Argentina’s 6,467 informal settlements, we can extrapolate from this ratio that the Census would count about 1.27 million households in Argentina’s informal settlements—a number strikingly close to the 1.24 million households reported by RENABAP.

A second way of doing this is to use something called [dasymetric mapping](https://www.epa.gov/enviroatlas/dasymetric-toolbox), which is a common spatial analysis approach to estimate how populations are distributed in space. Basically, instead of assuming that the population of a Census tract is evenly distributed throughout the area of the tract, we can use ancillary data like building footprints to estimate where in the tract the population lives. If, for example, 70% of the tract’s building footprints are clustered in the eastern half of the tract, and the tract has 100 families, we can estimate that 70 families probably live in that half of the tract, and 30 in the other half. (Incidentally, this technique was literally the reason I first started using building footprints in Argentina; research shows that [higher-resolution data like building footprints gives more precise estimates of flood risk](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-29094-x) than coarse datasets like census tracts.)

Interestingly, applying this approach to INDEC’s data results in *lower* estimates of population in informal settlements – about 997,000 Census households, or 3.37 million people – than the 1.27 million produced by the simpler, apples-to-apples comparison. This indicates that INDEC records more households per footprint in predominantly informal-settlement tracts than in the mixed and formal areas surrounding them. That pattern is consistent with informal-settlement buildings being more predominantly residential, but it does not independently establish how many households occupy each building. More on that below.

The takeaway here is that, in the Census tracts that correspond to Argentina’s informal settlements, INDEC’s household estimates are way below what we would expect them to be based on the number of building footprints. Whether we use the dasymetric mapping-implied 997,000 households or the 1.27 million households suggested by the simpler approach, INDEC appears to be missing roughly as many households as RENABAP, and potentially more.

**Yes, building footprints are a good proxy for households**

Specifically in informal settlements, [building footprints are actually a very good proxy for residential households](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29094-x). So good, in fact, that [RENABAP’s official documentation *explicitly* *requires*](https://www.argentina.gob.ar/sites/default/files/manual-para-la-conformacion-y-actualizacion-del-renabap.pdf) that the estimation of the number of inhabited dwellings in informal settlements be calculated in part by “a count of dwellings based on satellite imagery during the quality-control process.”

This has to do with the nature of informal settlements: they emerge because the [demand for housing far exceeds supply](https://unhabitat.org/the-challenge-of-slums-global-report-on-human-settlements-2003) (so, little to no vacancy), and informal settlements generally lack non-residential buildings, e.g., schools, offices, shopping centers, hospitals, etc. This is borne out by field surveys, too. Brazil’s 2022 Census, for instance, [surveyed more than 6.5 million dwellings in informal settlements](https://biblioteca.ibge.gov.br/visualizacao/livros/liv102134.pdf) and found that 85% were permanently occupied residential structures. Ethnographers in Argentina have shown that, in informal settlements in the Greater Buenos Aires area, vacancy rates are close to zero, to the point that [there’s even a subletting market](https://revistainvi.uchile.cl/index.php/INVI/article/view/62848) in some of these neighborhoods.

Does this mean that one building footprint equals one inhabited home? Not necessarily. Some buildings can be vacant, non-residential, or simply misidentified in satellite imagery. However, the opposite is also true: [a single building footprint can contain *multiple* households](https://doi.org/10.1186/1476-072X-12-4), either because it’s [a single-story, subdivided unit](https://portal.amelica.org/ameli/journal/80/805238006/html/), or a multi-story unit. A [2013 study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1476-072X-12-4) on the use of satellite imagery-detected building footprints in displaced persons’ camps documented several examples in Haiti where the number of households was nearly twice the number of detected building footprints. Specifically in Argentina, there are numerous reports of high-density, subdivided buildings in informal settlements (i.e., several households per building footprint), making it [very hard to estimate the true population](https://www.lanacion.com.ar/sociedad/golpeas-una-puerta-y-no-sabes-cuantas-familias-vas-a-encontrar-el-complejo-operativo-para-relevar-nid18052022/).

In my analysis, I handled this uncertainty by running sensitivity tests, meaning that I tested a range of possible assumptions about how many buildings are both occupied and residential. You can see the full table in [the working paper](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6588819), but the takeaways that are, even under deliberately conservative assumptions (filtering out all building footprints smaller than 10 square meters, assuming only 85% of remaining buildings are occupied homes, and applying RENABAP’s ratio of 1.1 families per dwelling), there are roughly 1.91 million households in Argentina’s informal settlements, compared to the 1.24 million reported by RENABAP. In order for RENABAP’s estimates to be correct, something like 41% of buildings in Argentina’s informal settlements would have to be vacant or non-residental (and this is without even considering the possibility that a single footprint could correspond to multiple households). As a consequence, my estimate is deliberately a conservative lower end, even though in reality I am most likely *still underestimating* the actual population of Argentina’s informal settlements.

**This is not as crazy as it sounds**

Counting people is hard. Really hard. Especially when you’re trying to count tens of millions of people. Even well-resourced census operations like the U.S. Census [frequently miss people](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/blogs/random-samplings/2023/10/understanding-undercounted-populations.html), which is why statistical agencies conduct independent [post-enumeration surveys](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2022/05/2020-census-undercount-overcount-rates-by-state.html) to measure how many people were missed or counted erroneously (something Argentina has not officially published since 1990 — more on this later). In recent years in Latin America, several countries have reported census enumeration shortfalls numbering in the millions, e.g., [4.1 million people in Colombia](https://www.dane.gov.co/files/censo2018/informacion-tecnica/cnpv-2018-omision-censal.pdf) (8.5%) in 2018, [1.9 million in Peru](https://censo2017.inei.gob.pe/inei-difunde-base-de-datos-de-los-censos-nacionales-2017-y-el-perfil-sociodemografico-del-peru/) (5.9%) in 2017, and [roughly 16.2 million net in Brazil](https://agenciadenoticias.ibge.gov.br/agencia-noticias/2012-agencia-de-noticias/noticias/41058-ibge-divulga-analise-de-cobertura-da-pesquisa-de-pos-enumeracao-do-censo-demografico-2022) (8.3%) in 2022\.

Counting people in informal settlements in particular is notoriously difficult. In São Paulo, one study warned that [census-reported favela populations were likely undercounted by about 50%](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0739456X211065495). A [2021 study of 118 informal settlements in Nigeria and Kenya](https://www.mdpi.com/2413-8851/5/2/48) found that even the most accurate of nine widely used population datasets missed an average of 61% of the field-referenced population. In India, the 2011 Census counted 65.5 million slum residents compared with a [government expert committee’s projection of 93.06 million](https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/PrintRelease.aspx?lang=2&reg=48&relid=71733)—a difference of 27.6 million people, or roughly 30%. 

In Argentina specifically, experts have been voicing serious concerns about census undercounts for years, especially in the context of informal settlements. In [a 2017 paper](https://www.scielo.org.mx/pdf/educm/v32n3/2448-6515-educm-32-03-00631.pdf), demographer Nicolás Sacco flagged INDEC’s own (officially unpublished) study that estimated a 7% omission rate in the 2001 census. Sacco also estimated that, per INDEC’s own housing data, there was a possible undercount in the 2010 Census on the scale of 6% of the population. (All this to say nothing of the severe and [widely-known political interference in INDEC’s operations](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/toolkits/good-statistical-practice/country-assessments/OECD-Assessment-of-the-Statistical-System-and-Key-Statistics-of-Argentina.pdf) from 2007 through 2015.) Going into the 2022 census, statisticians working for the City of Buenos Aires were [already warning of anticipated undercounts](https://www.clarin.com/ciudades/censo-2022-relevara-poblacion-villas-asentamientos-ciudad_0_Z3OMMd3cPq.html) in informal settlements and, during the census itself, [contemporary reporting](https://www.elcohetealaluna.com/si-no-lo-cuento-no-existe/) described thousands of families left waiting to be counted across several of the city’s largest villas. All of this is, in fact, the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the Argentine census – but I’m going to save the deep dive for the end of this post. What’s important for now is that, while a gap of three million people in Argentina’s national census might sound shocking, it is firmly within the realm of possibility.

**Maybe the population has actually just grown since the 2022 Census?**

I did my analysis in 2025, using 2024 data. The Census was conducted in 2022\. Is it possible that some combination of new construction, population growth, and migration could account for all these extra people?

We can actually assess new construction thanks to Google’s [Open Buildings Temporal](https://sites.research.google/gr/open-buildings/temporal/) dataset, which lets us compare how many buildings were in these Census tracts before the 2022 Census versus in the dataset that I used.

\[Show GIF of new construction, and also time series plot. Maybe los hornos again.\]

In the clean, mostly low-rise Census tracts I analyzed, buildings added after the 2022 Census account for at most about 20% of the excess building stock. In other words, most of the discrepancy was already present around the time of the Census. I can’t assume that the same 20% figure applies to every informal settlement in Argentina, but it strongly suggests that post-2022 construction is not enough to explain the gap on its own.

There’s also no evidence for some massive population surge after the 2022 Census or RENABAP’s data collection. INDEC reports Argentina’s population growth rate as [0.18% per year](https://www.indec.gob.ar/ftp/cuadros/publicaciones/proyecciones_nacionales_2022_2040.pdf), or roughly 250,000 people over three years. Even allowing for faster growth in informal settlements than elsewhere in the country, that’s not close to explaining a discrepancy on the scale of millions. Nor does net migration explain this. While Argentina has a sizable migrant population, I compared the [RENAPER register](https://www.argentina.gob.ar/sites/default/files/2022/12/08_-_caracterizacion_de_la_migracion_internacional.pdf) of foreign-born residents to [INDEC’s records](https://www.indec.gob.ar/indec/web/Institucional-GacetillaCompleta-481) and found, at most, a plausible undercount on the order of 10,000 to 250,000 people, which doesn’t come close to explaining the discrepancy we’re seeing (and, if it did, it would actually be further evidence of a Census undercount).

**So… could the Census be wrong?** 

Again, I want to be very clear: [it is *super* hard to do a national Census](https://greatdataproducts.com/episodes/2026/03/dick-demographic-data/). You won’t find a national census in any country that isn’t “wrong” in some way, and this post is emphatically not a criticism of the folks behind RENABAP or the INDEC Census. In fact, I would like nothing better than to get to work with them on integrating these data into their methods to help them do their work more accurately, faster, and cheaper. Please get in touch\!

That said, I want to talk about two ways in which the 2022 Census might be wrong. This is going to get complicated, so let me explain two key nuances. 

First, there’s a difference between knowing *how many* total people live in a country and knowing *where* those people actually live. Ideally, a Census does both, but it’s possible to get the first thing right and the second thing wrong. 

INDEC’s own documentation for the 2022 Census talks a lot about how difficult it was to figure out where people actually live. The 2022 Census was [the first *censo de derecho* in Argentina](https://redatam.indec.gob.ar/redarg/CENSOS/CPV2022/Docs/Redatam_aspectos_metodologicos.pdf), meaning the first one to try to assign people to their actual place of residence, rather than where they happened to be on Census Day. One consequence was that some people were initially recorded more than once—sometimes within the same dwelling and sometimes at different addresses—resulting in duplicate records. To get rid of these duplicates (including those resulting from duplicate addresses, but also from other causes), INDEC ended up [removing 4.8% of records from the 2022 Census](https://redatam.indec.gob.ar/redarg/CENSOS/CPV2022/Docs/Redatam_aspectos_metodologicos.pdf), equivalent to 2.2 million people. Importantly, there is no guarantee that this deduplication resulted in all of those people ultimately being assigned to the correct address; it is possible that a large number of people in the 2022 Census were recorded, but at the wrong address, which is one possible way that a roughly-correct national total could coexist with clearly incorrect local population counts.

INDEC also had to deal with records that [had no geographic information](https://redatam.indec.gob.ar/redarg/CENSOS/CPV2022/Docs/Redatam_aspectos_metodologicos.pdf). In these cases, they imputed an address based on either geocoding (in the case of digital survey responses) or operational forms maintained by the heads of the census tract. This is a standard operating procedure for censuses, but it is inherently approximate and, like deduplication, provides another way in which a person could be counted in the national census but not counted in the right place. Unlike deduplication, INDEC does not publish an estimate of how many records this affected.

This leads us to the second nuance I want to talk about. Basically, there’s a difference between a census being *internally consistent* versus one that is a *complete enumeration* of a country’s population. The former is a question of whether the new census matches up with sources like the previous census, and birth, death, and migration records. The latter is a question of whether everyone has actually been counted. Because internal consistency is really about “does your math make sense,” it is entirely possible for a census to be *internally consistent* while still failing to count large numbers of people. 

[INDEC’s demographic reconciliation of the 2022 Census](https://www.indec.gob.ar/ftp/cuadros/publicaciones/proyecciones_nacionales_2022_2040.pdf), published in 2025, gives us some insight into how this could happen. While they reported only a 0.5% net differential nationally, this was the sum of both undercounts and overcounts that offset each other, such as a 2.1% undercount of men nationally, which was partially offset by a 1.1% overcount of women. (INDEC also undercounted children under fourteen years old by 3.5%, and overcounted people ages 15 to 64 by 0.6%.) The deduplication we’ve just talked about is another version of this: duplicate records in the Census can offset missing records and lead to a “correct” national total – a rare case of two wrongs kind of making a right.

The problem with INDEC’s 2025 reconciliation is that it measures net demographic differences, *not* coverage completeness. [Standard census-evaluation practice](https://cdi.mecon.gob.ar/bases/doc/cepal/manual/74.pdf) distinguishes between indirect methods like demographic reconciliation and direct measurement through a post-enumeration survey, which independently estimates how many people were missed or counted incorrectly. The importance of that distinction is especially clear in Argentina’s 2001 Census. INDEC conducted a post-enumeration survey across 26 urban areas but never published its results. According to [Nicolás Sacco](https://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?pid=S0186-72102017000300631&script=sci_arttext), the unpublished survey found omission of roughly 7%—more than twice the 2.75% suggested by INDEC’s demographic reconciliation. (And Sacco’s own analysis of the 2010 Census, remember, estimated omission as high as 6%.) INDEC has not published post-enumeration-survey results since the 1991 Census, and it conducted no national post-enumeration survey after the 2010 or 2022 censuses. Consequently, although Argentina’s censuses have generally been demographically consistent, we do not have a reliable direct measure of how completely the two most recent censuses counted Argentina’s population.

While we don’t have affirmative evidence that the 2022 Census *was* complete, there’s a lot of evidence suggesting that it *was not*. INDEC reports that [98.6% of planned Census segments were covered](https://redatam.indec.gob.ar/redarg/CENSOS/CPV2022/Docs/Redatam_aspectos_metodologicos.pdf) by the 2022 Census; it did not publish the locations of the remaining 1.4%. When INDEC reopened data collection after Census Day to recover missing records, contemporary reporting documented [29,320 previously uncensused dwellings recovered in the first day alone](https://censo.gob.ar/index.php/censo-2022-resultados-provisorios-de-acuerdo-a-la-tendencia-de-campo/), while INDEC [acknowledged that some population remained uncensused](https://www.rionegro.com.ar/politica/censo-2022-marco-lavagna-aseguro-que-es-muy-chica-la-porcion-de-poblacion-sin-censar-2306041/). 

There are also especially strong reasons to think that these omissions were concentrated in informal settlements. As I mentioned earlier in this post, [Buenos Aires’s own statistics officials were already warning](https://www.clarin.com/ciudades/censo-2022-relevara-poblacion-villas-asentamientos-ciudad_0_Z3OMMd3cPq.html) prior to the 2022 Census that their existing projections for the city’s informal settlements — 227,597 people living in 63,378 dwellings — were probably too low. The city ended up designing a special operation for those neighborhoods, coordinating with officials and community workers with previous experience conducting census there. In Villa 21-24 alone, the Census deployed [1,300 enumerators to cover just 35 blocks and roughly 40,000 people](https://www.lanacion.com.ar/sociedad/golpeas-una-puerta-y-no-sabes-cuantas-familias-vas-a-encontrar-el-complejo-operativo-para-relevar-nid18052022/). As *La Nación* reported, the difficulty was not merely finding the buildings: several households could live behind what appeared from outside to be a single dwelling, in buildings reaching five stories and dense networks of internal passages. Reporting on earlier censuses in Buenos Aires villas documented [landlords preventing census workers from recording their tenants](https://www.lanacion.com.ar/buenos-aires/propietarios-vs-inquilinos-la-cruda-disputa-viviendas-nid2379868/), and residents and neighborhood organizations said those problems happened again in 2022\. In the days immediately following Census Day, [housing-rights advocates reported](https://www.elcohetealaluna.com/si-no-lo-cuento-no-existe/) that thousands of families across Villa 20, Villa 21-24, Barrio INTA, Ramón Carrillo, Ricciardelli and other barrios had waited all day without a census worker arriving.

Perhaps the strongest evidence of undercounting is the case of an informal settlement in Buenos Aires, Barrio Padre Ricciardelli. In 2026, [IDECBA compared INDEC’s own Census field-summary sheets with final Census data](https://www.estadisticaciudad.gob.ar/eyc/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Los_barrios_populares_BaPls_2002_2022_parte_01.pdf) and found that the published Census data reported only 1,118 dwellings and 3,640 people versus 4,906 dwellings and 23,213 people *recorded in INDEC’s own field survey material*. IDECBA describes the difference  — 3,788 dwellings and 19,573 people missing — as “subenumeración u omisión censal.” Meanwhile, INDEC’s own reconciliation for the entirety of CABA differs from the Census by only 757 people, showing how an internally consistent reconciliation can entirely overlook omissions of that magnitude.

**Where does this leave us?**

Even under deliberately conservative estimates of population based on building footprints, and even accounting for factors like population growth, migration, and new construction, there is no obvious way to reconcile RENABAP or INDEC’s official numbers with what appears to be an undercount on the scale of roughly three million people. These findings are also consistent with similar situations in other Latin American countries and with the testimony and analyses of experts in Argentina (to say nothing of the residents of informal settlements themselves). And because INDEC has not produced an official post-enumeration survey since 1991, it starts to look very plausible that the 2022 Census may actually be missing millions of people.

What happens next is up to the folks at RENABAP and INDEC. There’s not much more I can do with public data – and anyway, my goal was never to replace the census. I originally started this work to show that building footprints were a useful supplement to get a more precise understanding of where people live in informal settlements in order to protect them from flooding and, more broadly, to show that data sources like building footprints can be incredibly useful in supporting municipal planning *and* efforts like a national census. So my hope, as I said earlier in this post and elsewhere, is to get more people using these data to help improve our understanding of things like flood risk and, yes, also to make sure everyone in Argentina is counted.

For the new material, there are four things you want to add. The first is to move the section about new construction earlier in the post and to present it as the reason the method exists rather than as a problem you have to rule out. The census only happens once every ten years, but buildings in informal settlements go up every year, and this approach lets you see those changes as they happen. The second is to mention that newer building datasets now include height, and that height data is the obvious next step for figuring out how many households a single building actually contains. The third is to argue that Argentina should go back to doing post-enumeration surveys, since there has not been one since 1990\. The fourth is to add a few sentences about surveillance near the end of the post. You want to acknowledge that some people would rather not be counted by the state and that this is a legitimate political position, but then point out that this method counts buildings rather than people, that the data is already publicly available, and that what actually happens when people are not counted is that emergency planners have no idea how many people live on a given block when a flood comes.

For framing, the issue is that the ending of the post says the goal was to build a useful tool, while the title and the opening say the census is missing millions of people. Those are two different stories, and right now the top of the post tells one and the bottom tells the other. It is worth thinking about whether the title and the opening should sound more like the ending.
